newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian coalition breaks stalemate over jobs law.
newsitem.headline: Italian coalition breaks stalemate over jobs law.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government struck a deal on Thursday with parliamentary ally Communist Refoundation over disputed employment issues, easing tensions within the troubled coalition.

Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni told reporters that the accord, reached after a four hour meeting between the heads of coalition parties and Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, had strengthened the 10-month-old government.
"There is political solidarity in the (parliamentary) majority and this coalition confirms that it intends to last for the entire legislature," Veltroni said.
Bertinotti said the deal meant that 100,000 new jobs would be created for young people in the underdeveloped south.

"The stalemate and division that had arisen within the majority has been unblocked," Bertinotti said in a statement. "The problem of employment is so dramatic that we need to do something constructive immediately. This we can now do."

Refoundation, which holds the balance of power in the lower house of parliament, infuriated coalition parties this week by threatening to scupper a new jobs initiative being prepared by Prime Minister Romano Prodi's cabinet.

The argument was the latest in a series of flare-ups with Refoundation, leaving some coalition allies to privately question whether they should continue to court the support of the small, hardline party.
The leader of the centre-right opposition, former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, said on Thursday the government looked secure, despite the bickering.
"The forces of the left might argue, but they will never let this coalition fall," Berlusconi told reporters.

He added that Prodi's government was at more risk from centrist parties within the coalition. "It could fall if moderates understand that they are distancing themselves from their principles and from their electorate," he said.
A senior politician from the government told Reuters this week that some coalition partners wanted to ditch Refoundation and link up with centrist parties in the Berlusconi bloc.
"Unfortunately we are far from reaching that sort of deal. There is no alternative to the current set-up," he said, declining to be named.

Prodi still faces the difficult task of persuading Bertinotti to accept a further dose of tough budgetary medicine needed to give Italy a chance of becoming a founding member of planned European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Refoundation has already said it will block any cuts to welfare spending or fresh tax hikes, raising the threat of another clash with Prodi.

Nonetheless, Thursday's accord should help clear the air for a while. Under the terms of the deal, the government said it would release funds for jobs creation schemes in the south, but refused to drop plans to encourage new temporary work contracts.
According to latest data some 12.2 percent of the Italian workforce is without a job, and unions have accused the government of dragging its feet over the problem.

Labour Minister Tiziano Treu introduced an employment bill to parliament earlier this month, which includes provisions aimed at cutting the working week, introducing more flexible work contracts and boosting apprenticeship schemes.
